I have completed the second season of Saga of Tanya the Evil and I gave it a 7/10 It’s been a while, but The Saga of Tanya the Evil is finally back with a brand-new season. After rewatching the first season as a refresher, I came away from this one feeling both a little distracted and genuinely interested at the same time. At first glance that sounds contradictory, but it actually makes a lot of sense. What I considered the biggest flaw of the first season has become this season’s greatest strength, yet it also creates a new problem: Tanya now feels like a side character inher own anime. She is, quite literally, a soldier carrying out orders from her superiors. This season is all about the bigger picture. War and politics take center stage, and Tanya mainly serves as a lens through which we see different aspects of the conflict, whether it’s life on the home front, the planning of offensives, or the morale of the enemy.

The real focus lies with the Empire’s generals, Hans von Zettour and Kurt von Rudersdorf, as they search for an exit strategy to bring the war to an end. Along the way they have to deal with the government’s objectives, the struggle on the eastern front, and the neutral nation of Ildoa (the in-world counterpart of the Kingdom of Italy).

I really enjoy the contrast between the fictional universe and how closely it mirrors real history between 1914 and 1945. That’s one of the anime’s biggest strengths, alongside its excellent animation and soundtrack. We see far less of Being X (God) this time around; he only shows up briefly at the end, but it makes for a pretty good cliffhanger.

The other thing that kept me interested is the season’s central theme: how to end a war, and how differently that question looks from a military perspective versus a political one. Ending a war is easy. Negotiating favorable terms is the hard part, especially when it means giving up territory or paying reparations. It made me think of today’s Russia–Ukraine war. For Russia, ending the war is extremely difficult, because the humiliation of a bad deal is arguably the worst outcome, so it seeks a major victory as its exit strategy. That’s exactly what the Empire does in this season.

Overall, this is a solid continuation of The Saga of Tanya the Evil. Its different approach brings something fresh, but if the story is going to improve, it needs to bring the focus back to Tanya herself.

I DON'T NEED TO SEE THE PANTY COLLECTION OF EVERY SINGLE FEMALE CHARACTER IN THE ENTIRE CAST TO APPRECIATE A WORK OF FICTION! And that's how this review begins, because I genuinely don't understand... Why turn a zombie apocalypse survival series into an ECCHI?! I'm not entirely against this genre, even though it doesn't interest me, but some works simply don't need it... It's just counterproductive. It undermines the seriousness of the story and the sense of gravity surrounding the events. The female characters are degraded, constantly being shown in their panties and bent over as far as physically possible. How am I supposed to take thesecharacters seriously when they actually had some potential?

Honestly, the first five episodes showed promise. Sure, there were already a few questionable moments, with panties here and there and Shizuka's assets going "Boing Boing" with every step she takes, but it was manageable. The main characters seemed interesting: Saeko, Takashi, Rei, Kota, Saya... They all seemed to have hidden depths that could gradually be explored as the story progressed.

Then we get to episode 6, and that's where everything goes downhill...

An almost entire episode where you get to enjoy the four main female characters taking an uncensored bath together while getting drunk, only to then start making advances toward the two main male characters. JUST WHY?!

And then comes episode 7, where the female characters obviously haven't had time to get dressed again, so they spend the entire episode in their panties. What a coincidence!

I understand that for some aspiring authors, making ecchi or hentai content can be an easier way to sell their work. But doing this in a series like this one, which had the potential to feature interesting, well-developed characters and a promising story and plot on paper, is just a waste. Even if I do think the story drags on for too long and takes far too much time to actually reveal anything meaningful to us. (Then again, when you dedicate an entire episode to showing all your female characters naked, you're not exactly helping your own case...)

Of course, I'd vaguely heard of Highschool of the Dead before watching it, mainly because of that infamous scene where Takashi uses Rei's breasts to help him aim his sniper rifle. Honestly, I expected to laugh when I finally saw that scene in context. But the problem is that the series has gone SO overboard with the sexualization of its female characters that, by that point, it just disgusted me even more. My only reaction was basically, "Here we go again with another pointless scene..."

Because that's the real problem: showing some of a character's intimate side isn't ALWAYS a bad thing. It can help bring complicated romances to a conclusion or sometimes serve a comedic purpose, particularly in lighter series.

But in a work like this one, which isn't trying to be a comedy, doesn't develop any romantic relationships, and aims to be gory, tragic, and occasionally dark, sexualizing its characters serves NO PURPOSE WHATSOEVER. It adds absolutely nothing to the story, other than giving horny teenagers the chance to fantasize about being in Takashi's shoes.

In my opinion, this series is a massive waste of potential. That being said, I do want to give credit to the animation, which is genuinely impressive for a 2010 production, with some remarkably ambitious shots for its time. The action scenes are still pretty engaging, and that's what kept me hooked during the first five episodes. I also appreciate the zombie outbreak premise, which isn't just a copy of The Walking Dead, as some people claim. After all, the manga dates back to 2006...

You'll like it if: • You enjoy traveller adventures with a bit of mystery. • You like dark and twisted themes wrapped in an otherwise cute-looking anime. • You enjoy watching a group of misfits come together, help each other, and embark on a quest of self-discovery. • You appreciate atmospheric environments. You won't like it if: • You have a strong aversion to lolicon or anything associated with it. • You have a strong aversion to what can sometimes only be described as torture p*. • You prefer a large main cast with complex, intertwined relationships.• Dark and twisted shows really aren't your thing.

Story: Made in Abyss Season 1 is essentially the story of two kids embarking on a journey into, well, the Abyss. Along the way, we learn more about the secrets hidden within its different levels, as well as the pasts and origins of our main characters. Personally, I really liked the build-up to the journey, and I thoroughly enjoyed the almost game-level-like exploration of the Abyss, with all the weird environments, creatures, and individuals each level has to offer. The twists get progressively darker, and certain moments are particularly intense, especially considering the ages of the characters. Some scenes and dialogues are also surprisingly explicit given their ages, without really contributing much to the plot, which is... a choice.

Characters: Our main characters are Riko and Reg, so if you don't like them for whatever reason, you're really out of luck, since they remain the main focus for most of the season. Or maybe you're in luck, because you'll get to see them suffer for most of it (?) Hopefully, you're not that kind of person. Regardless, I think they're pretty solid main characters, each with their own motivations, strengths, and flaws, all of which are explored adequately throughout the season. Their bond is also very cute. The supporting cast is interesting as well, with some really peculiar characters who help push the story forward. One character we get to know better later in the journey also receives some solid exploration and development.

Art & Sound: The environmental design is phenomenal. The colours and scenery are simply magical. Certain character designs are hard to translate from the manga to the anime, like Ozen's, but, overall, they did the best they could. The OST is also really strong, especially when "Hanezeve Caradhina" starts playing. I get chills. It's that good.

Personal enjoyment: Made in Abyss is a well-paced, visually stunning adventure with sympathetic characters, captivating mystery and a fascinating world to explore. That said, there are some aspects that give me the ick and prevent me from enjoying the show as much as I otherwise could have. These mostly come down to a few really random and unnecessary suggestive shots and dialogues, as well as moments of suffering and humiliation that made me question whether they were actually necessary to convey what the characters were feeling or whether they were, to put it the way people often do, the author's barely disguised fetish. So yeah, while I appreciate the show for what it offers as a dark adventure, I wouldn't wholeheartedly recommend it without this disclaimer. Some of its "creative choices" genuinely made me question my enjoyment of the show at times.

entry.title: Tsuihou sareta Tensei Juukishi wa Game Chishiki de Musou suru

results.review:
Definitely recommend waiting until all the episodes are out before watching this one instead of keeping up with the weekly releases. So yes, this story is another fantasy, sorta isekai anime. It's set in a world where characters have stats and level up like in a video game. From my understanding, our MC Elyma's soul essentially merged with the soul of someone from this world. Or at least, that's how I interpreted it. The anime depicts it as Elyma suddenly remembering his past life one day, realizing that he's been reincarnated into a world that resembles a game he used to play, but still retains thememory of the person who's body he's in. Though he's both people I think? It's a bit confusing to explain lol.

With his knowledge of the game, his ultimate goal is to become the strongest person in the world by using what he believes is the strongest class, the Heavy Knight. However, everyone else looks down on Heavy Knights because they have a reputation for being a weak class. Despite that, Elyma is determined to prove otherwise, growing stronger and gaining allies along the way, including Ruche, who is a Pierrot.

Now, while I do have mixed feelings about this anime, I ultimately really like it! Ruche's reactions alone make it so enjoyable to watch lol. The animation is definitely different, with a lot of interesting high and low camera angles that give it a unique feel. I also really like the art style, especially how flowy everyone's hair looks. It's such a small detail, but I love how it looks on all the characters.

Unfortunately, there's one MAJOR thing I dislike about this anime, and that's the FREAKIN RECAPS!

Like, okay, a minute long recap at the beginning of an episode? Sure, that's understandable. But 5–10 MINUTES?! Guys, that's practically half the episode already! And if that wasn't enough, they even throw in 1-2 minute long recaps during what would normally be the commercial breaks, reminding us of something that LITERALLY JUST HAPPENED!

Like, come on! We JUST watched that!

This is exactly why I recommend waiting until the entire season is finished before watching it that way you can just skip the recaps. When you're watching weekly, you barely get any actual story progression because so much of the episode is spent recapping things we've already seen. It really hurts the pacing, especially when you're excited to see what happens next.

But yes, aside from that little rant, I genuinely do enjoy this anime. I like the characters, the world, and the overall story. It's just frustrating because I feel like it could've been so much better without all those unnecessary recaps.

Opening and Ending Music:

The openings are a bit skippable for me, not gonna lie. They're not bad, but they don't really stand out to me either. The first ending, though? I REALLY like it! They had ReoNa singing it, and I already love her music, so that was definitely a plus for me. I also like the second ending, but man, the first one is just so good lol.

Overall: Good anime with an enjoyable story, likable characters, and a unique art style. I would honestly consider reading the manga because I do like the story that much. However, the anime REALLY needs to fix its recap problem. It takes away so much from what could otherwise be a much better experience.

Despite my complaints, I still enjoyed it and would recommend giving it a watch, just preferably after the season finishes airing.

7/10

Before getting into my review of Ghost in the Shell 2026, I should preface this by saying that I haven't read the original Ghost in the Shell manga, which I'm told this new anime is a pretty much one-to-one adaptation of. So I'm going into this based on what I already know about the franchise, which is all the previous anime adaptations, minus Ghost in the Shell: SAC_2045. I'm essentially viewing this as its own, no pun intended, standalone iteration of Ghost in the Shell. That being said, Ghost in the Shell 2026 is a pretty solid show. It's got all the things you'd expect fromGhost in the Shell — or, at least, all the things I'd expect. Plenty of robots, telepathic conversations through the net, guns, action, jargon, technobabble. It's all here. And for the most part, this feels very much in the spirit of the previous adaptations.

The main difference with this new series is its much brighter, more playful art style. There's a lot more humour and visual gags in this version of Ghost in the Shell. Some of it works, some of it doesn't, but the overall visual aesthetic is really strong. The action sequences are some of the best in the entire franchise, and even the more mundane dialogue scenes are animated with this really bouncy, fluid quality to them. I think you could appreciate this show purely for its visuals alone. It's very much in line with what you'd expect from a modern anime, and it's clearly trying to appeal to a contemporary audience.

On that note, though, like a lot of modern anime, this series is fast-paced. And I think that's one of my main criticisms of the show. Some people might see that as a benefit, but, man, this thing moves at breakneck speed. Sometimes that works in its favour, particularly during the action sequences, but it's not quite as effective when characters are firing exposition and technobabble at you every five seconds.

I can just about keep up with what's going on, and I think a big part of that is because I already have some familiarity with the Ghost in the Shell franchise. But I can easily imagine newcomers being completely overwhelmed by the sheer amount of information being thrown at them, often without much time to process any of it. And I don't think that's necessarily what this show wants to do. Given its glossy presentation, vibrant art style and hyperactive animation, I get the impression that it's trying to make Ghost in the Shell more accessible to modern anime audiences. But I'm not entirely sure how those audiences are going to respond to a writing style that's, in some ways, quite retro.

Going back to the pacing, I also think it prevents the series from exploring its ideas in as much depth as previous iterations. I think it was around episode four where we get this big action sequence, followed by an existential conversation involving the Tachikomas, and then, before you know it, we're exploring Motoko's own existential questions about life. All of this happens within the space of a single episode.

Compare that to something like Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex, where I could easily imagine each of those ideas getting an episode of its own. And while Stand Alone Complex could certainly be self-indulgent at times, I think it benefited from that willingness to slow down and really sit with its ideas.

I also think the darker tone of Stand Alone Complex helped when it came to exploring the more psychologically and philosophically complex aspects of the franchise. It gave those conversations room to breathe, allowing the series to properly dig into questions about consciousness, identity and what it actually means to be human.

This new series, by comparison, doesn't seem particularly interested in dwelling on those ideas for much of its runtime. It's more concerned with flashy visuals, action and comedic gags, and it's not really until the end of the series that it starts leaning heavily into the philosophical discussions and exposition that I'd traditionally associate with Ghost in the Shell. And by the end of the show, it didn't feel as impactful as a previous iterations. or maybe I've just seen these ideas too many times now and I'm desensitised.

And that's really my biggest criticism of the show. It's just too fast and too flashy compared to what I'm used to from this franchise. I don't necessarily think that's an inherently bad direction to take, but I do think something gets lost in the process.

Apart from that, though, I think this is a solid new take on Ghost in the Shell. If you're a long-time fan who hasn't watched this series yet, I think your enjoyment is ultimately going to come down to personal preference. As I mentioned earlier, I haven't read the original manga, so I can't really comment on how faithfully this adapts the source material. I have no idea how it compares to the manga on that front. A unique and seriously shocking anime! Rewatching Grisaia no Kajitsu, I was less surprised by the events, after all, I was already familiar with many of the plot twists and the story's most impactful moments. However, this doesn't diminish the gravity of what the series presents. Grisaia is undeniably a shocking anime; it isn't afraid to tackle disturbing situations or subject its characters to extremely traumatic experiences. It’s one of those shows that might start off seeming relatively ordinary, but as the episodes progress, it reveals a narrative that is far heavier and more complex than it initially appeared. In this first season, the focus is primarilyon the girls at the school and their respective pasts. Yuuji, our protagonist, serves as the connecting thread between these stories, helping to flesh out each character's individual conflicts. Since the source material is a visual novel with branching paths, adapting it into a linear narrative couldn't have been an easy task. After all, it requires condensing events, rearranging elements, and finding a way to introduce multiple characters without completely compromising their story arcs. Even so, I believe the adaptation did an excellent job within those constraints, delivering a satisfying experience while preserving much of the events' emotional impact.

One of the most interesting aspects is precisely how the series handles the girls' pasts. At first, they might seem like characters representing fairly standard archetypes, but as their stories unfold, we realize there is much more beneath the surface of their personalities and behaviors. Each one carries her own struggles, traumas, and conflicts, and it is this exploration that makes certain revelations so powerful. Not every story resonated with me in the same way, but I find it fascinating how the series transforms what could have been run-of-the-mill characters into far more complex figures.

The animation also deserves a mention. Although the character designs aren't particularly revolutionary, the quality of the animation makes for a very pleasant visual experience. The movement, expressions, and the way certain scenes are constructed demonstrate a level of care that deserves recognition. Making characters with relatively conventional designs work so well on screen, conveying emotion and carrying dramatic moments, is an achievement that shouldn't be overlooked. Furthermore, the direction successfully shifts between everyday moments, comedy, and extremely heavy situations, creating contrasts that help define the work's identity.

Narratively, however, is where Grisaia truly stands out. This is an anime that tackles themes such as death, abuse, violence, psychological trauma, and various other sensitive issues. Some scenes are particularly disturbing, and the way certain events are presented can be quite unsettling. It isn't a series I would recommend indiscriminately, as the content might be too heavy for some viewers. At the same time, I believe this willingness to explore extreme situations is one of the traits that makes the series so memorable, even if the execution of its dramatic elements isn't always perfect.

It is also worth noting that, despite the presence of ecchi elements, reducing Grisaia to just that aspect would mean ignoring much of what the series has to offer. Yes, there are moments of fanservice, suggestive situations, and tropes typical of the genre, but these are far from being the narrative's main draw. If you came here expecting only provocative scenes, there is a good chance you will be surprised by the direction the story takes. The ecchi shares the stage with drama, tragedy, mystery, and action, creating a rather unique blend.

Overall, I find Grisaia no Kajitsu to be a memorable experience, primarily due to its ability to surprise the viewer and explore the darker sides of its characters. Even while rewatching the series and already knowing the key plot points, I was able to appreciate its qualities once more and understand why it remains so memorable to me. There are issues with the adaptation, and some narrative choices might be divisive, but overall, I believe the strengths outweigh the flaws.

If you are looking for a work that blends ecchi, psychological drama, tragedy, and action, Grisaia could be a great choice. Just don't expect a lighthearted or conventional experience, as this story can be much heavier than it appears at first glance.

Recommended.

I think one of the best things about the dub is how much personality the voice actors bring to their characters. Even after already watching the sub and knowing what was going to happen, the dub made the experience feel fresh all over again. The delivery of certain lines, the little changes inemotion, and the chemistry between the characters really made everything come to life. It's always a treat hearing these familiar voices again, especially when the cast clearly puts so much effort into their performances.

Of course the animation was amazing. I love seeing the girls in One Piece get their own little spin off and side stories. I’m excited for more of the Heroine series.

One Piece has such an incredible cast of female characters, and I feel like they don't always get enough time to shine outside of the main story. That's what makes this series so refreshing! It's nice seeing these characters in a different setting, getting to explore their personalities, relationships, and experiences without everything revolving around Luffy and the Straw Hats' next big adventure. These smaller stories might not have the same stakes as the main series, but they have so much heart and charm.

I also love how this feels like a celebration of the One Piece world itself. There's so much more to this universe than just the main adventure, and it's exciting to see Toei exploring those possibilities. The beautiful animation, expressive character designs, and attention to detail make this feel like more than just a little bonus episode. You can really appreciate how much love went into bringing these stories to life.

Honestly, I would happily watch an entire season of episodes like this. Whether it's Nami, Robin, or some of the other amazing women in One Piece, there are so many characters who deserve their own spotlight. I hope this is just the beginning because I would love to see more of these fun, heartfelt, and character-driven stories animated.

And as someone who loves the English dub, getting to hear the cast again is just the cherry on top. Watching the sub and dub back to back reminded me why I love both versions so much. They each bring something special to the experience, and I couldn't be happier that we're getting more One Piece content like this.

results.review:
Another recap episode. Personally, I’m not a big fan of recap episodes, and Maoyuu Maou Yuusha: Kono Monogatari wa, Niku dake de wa Nai no ja! is no exception. As the name implies, this is a special that gathers events previously shown in the series, summarizing episodes 1 through 9. In other words, there is no new story here, let alone any significant character development. The goal is simply to look back at the show's key events up to that point, serving as a summary for the viewer. However, despite usually disliking this type of content, I have to admit that this recap went down a biteasier for me. I think this was mainly because I enjoy Maoyuu Maou Yuusha, and since it had been quite a while since I last watched the anime, revisiting some of its events was actually pleasant. Rewatching certain scenes and being reminded of the characters stirred up a sense of nostalgia, making the experience a bit more interesting than I had initially expected.

Still, it is important to note that how much you enjoy it depends heavily on the circumstances in which you watch the special. For someone who has just finished the previous episodes, or who is currently watching the series and decides to view the recap right after the events it covers, there is hardly any real appeal here. After all, you are essentially rewatching scenes that are still fresh in your memory without getting anything new in return. In that context, the episode becomes extremely redundant and can even disrupt the viewing flow, breaking the story's continuity to present content the viewer already knows.

On the other hand, when there has been a significant gap since you last watched the show, the recap can end up being a bit more enjoyable. That is precisely what happened in my case. Since I didn't remember all the details very clearly, revisiting the events of the first nine episodes was a reasonably interesting way to refresh my memory and recall some of the reasons why I liked the series. I wouldn't call it a particularly exciting experience, but at least I was able to enjoy the content without feeling like I was just wasting my time.

The issue is that this merit stems far more from my fondness for the show and the time that had passed since I first watched it than from the quality of the special itself. A recap is still a recap, and this one offers no major new insights, deeper analysis, or previously unseen scenes that would justify its existence for someone already following the story. It is supplementary material that might be useful in certain situations, but it is far from essential.

Overall, Maoyuu Maou Yuusha: Kono Monogatari wa, Niku dake de wa Nai no ja! isn't exactly a bad special, but I wouldn't consider it particularly good either. I managed to enjoy the experience because I like the series and appreciated the chance to revisit events that had grown a bit hazy in my memory. Even so, I acknowledge that for most viewers watching the recap during or immediately after the series, it will likely seem quite disposable.

Raiting: 5/10.

Just not a good show. The characters are flat and 1-dimensional (Lotte: Twilight lover, Sucy: mushroom lover, Constanze: robot lover, etc.). The main character, Akko, doesn't develop at all during the series, except a tiny bit at the end. But, even as she progresses through events that require her to use a specific virtue, she quickly regresses the very next episode. For the greater part of 24 episodes, she remains an impatient, lazy, shortcut-seeking character with no real motivation other than wanting to meet the person she idolizes. Nothing about "saving the witching world" or "power of friendship", just that one reason. Was her lifesaved by this person? Nope, she just saw a performance once. 

These regressions are even pointed out by the side characters episode by episode. Worse, her foil, Diana, is actually a well-written character who is shown to be a resilient, hard-worker with an unrivaled passion for magic. There's nothing that Akko bests her at, yet Akko is the hand-wavy chosen one.

It's a poorly constructed cast of characters and a plot that ends up relying in their ignorance and character flaws to progress logically. These character flaws are unaddressed in side characters, and never truly resolved in the main characters. It's as if the intended audience was for younger kids, but they forgot to include any of the lessons or morals within the writing that is typical of shows aimed at a young audience.

If you liked the original one-offs for Little Witch Academia, you may still enjoy this. But consider giving it a very short leash. I regret giving it as long a leash as I did.

One of Vinland Saga's most impressive feats to me is setting up the character of Askeladd the same way many other shows introduce the main antagonist of the story, he arrives, ruins Thorfinns life and serves as his main driving factor to become stronger and achieve his goal... But after simply spending time with Askelladds character you cant help but love him, although hes meant to portray violence and the cruel side of humanity at the beginning of the show, overtime you start to justify what hes doing and learn his real thoughts on violence. He isnt a good person in the slightest, but hesalso not pretending to be.

Thorfinn on the other hand is a really interesting character because you want to root for him since hes the MC, but we know what hes doing and trying to achieve is all pointless, his thirst for revenge will lead only to more sorrow and violence that his father tried so hard to teach him was wrong. Not letting him achieve his dream of revenge after using it as something to cling to for basically his whole life up until this point is brutal, since without that part of him he now has nothing.

When it comes to the presentation of the show its really mixed honestly, Some of the environments are really well drawn and capture the grey misery of England. But the show also has alot of CGI which isnt awful but isnt pretty either. 

The soundtrack was super weird to me, there is one scene which stood out to me where Askeladd is torturing someone and the ost is just some straight bullshit it actually had me pausing to see if i had a tab open. Its usually alright though, nothing special really.

The only thing not misleading about this show's title is that it does in fact take place in Kowloon. There is nothing generic about this show and the only romance involved kicks in about halfway through the very last episode. Kowloon Generic Romance is very much a psychological mystery story. It sort of reminds me of Twin Peaks in the way that it first appears to the viewer as a normal town but then the onion starts unpeeling and things just get weirder and weirder. By the end of it things are Evangelion levels of surreal and the whole thing pays off in quite a satisfyingway. 

The only real issue I have with this anime is that it's about 10 episodes of setup that all eventually does pay off iin the end, but it takes forever to get there. I didn't particularly like any of the characters immediately and the show, while interesting enough to keep me from dropping it, felt like it was treading water for a long time. It feels like they had the ending all planned out and then wrote the rest of the show backwards. They're very purposeful about slow dripping the plot to you just enough to keep you coming back. It takes you on a ride of "wtf is this show even about" to "oh wow this might be a masterpiece", but the climb to the top of the hill is uneven and only ramps up towards the end.

Other than that, there's not much else to say without giving away spoilers. The music in the show is solid and the OP and ED are both catchy and fit the series. There's some cool modern takes on sexuality in the show that set it apart from a lot of older series. The art and animation aren't epic or anything but are definitely quality and above and beyond what was needed to pull off the story. The characters are deep and the world building (at least of Kowloon) is pretty good. No complaints on the voice acting.

All in all, I'd say just watch it if you are even slightly interested. I wouldn't say it's "must watch" but it's just below that tier for me. I think with some pacing changes it could have been better, but it's still way above average and I can already tell I'll be thinking about this series for a while. this anime had been sitting on my plan to watch for ages, and holy fucking shit, what an absolute mess. i expected a mediocre romance at worst, but i wasn't prepared for something that feels like the product of a horny, misogynistic preteen who has absolutely no idea how women or the real world work. the first episode is already bizarre, introducing a situation involving sexual harassment that eventually turns into the male lead getting to play the romantic savior. but somehow, the second episode manages to make everything even worse when this same guy repeatedly kisses the protagonist after she explicitly says she doesn't wanthim to. and we're supposed to find this romantic? what the actual fuck? the fact that he's the male lead doesn't magically make his behavior acceptable.

A bit cliché, but fun to watch! Tokyo Ravens is an anime that blends fantasy, action, and the supernatural, featuring a story about onmyouji, magical techniques, and spirits, with plenty of battles between those who wield such powers. To put it briefly, that’s pretty much the gist of it. While the premise has some interesting elements, the show quickly reveals that it follows a very familiar genre structure, recycling ideas seen in many other anime. Even so, despite all those clichés, I ended up enjoying the experience. The narrative features a set of very common tropes: two female characters interested in the protagonist, a friend within hisinner circle, and, of course, the classic arc of a weak character gradually discovering his true potential. It’s essentially a collection of familiar ideas, and you’re unlikely to find anything truly groundbreaking here. However, I don't think a show needs to reinvent the wheel to be entertaining, and Tokyo Ravens makes good use of its elements to craft an engaging story.

The plot is relatively predictable at times, yet it offers enough interesting moments to hold my attention. The supernatural setting also gives the show a distinct identity, particularly through the battle techniques and the unique traits of the magic users. While I wouldn't call the world-building exceptional, the premise holds interesting potential, and the series explores it satisfactorily for anyone looking for a fantasy anime packed with action and a few mysteries along the way.

Another aspect that really enhanced my experience was the cast. The characters are incredibly charismatic, and their interactions make the story much more enjoyable. Even when the plot falls back on predictable situations, following this group remains fun. For me, this is one of the work's greatest strengths: it manages to make well-worn tropes work thanks to how it introduces its characters and develops their relationships with one another.

The comedy also deserves a mention. There are genuinely funny moments, and the humor helps balance out the narrative's more serious aspects. I particularly enjoy the interactions between Harutora and Kon; they share a great dynamic that leads to some of the anime's funniest situations. Kon, in fact, is a character worth highlighting on her own. While her appearance and behavior lean toward the "mascot" archetype, she isn't limited to that role. When the story calls for it, she makes meaningful contributions, proving that her presence offers more than just cute or comic relief.

As for the animation, I’d say it’s average but gets the job done. It doesn't exactly dazzle visually, yet it is competent enough to make the action scenes enjoyable to watch. In my opinion, the biggest issue lies in the use of 3D animation. At times, the contrast between the traditional style and the 3D elements is glaring, creating a visual disconnect that I found bothersome. I felt the integration could have been handled better, though it didn't completely ruin the experience for me.

Overall, Tokyo Ravens may not stand out for its originality, but it makes up for that with a charismatic cast, solid comedy, and a plot that, while predictable, is fun to follow. I wouldn't call it an exceptional anime or a genre-defining masterpiece, but I do believe it delivers a highly satisfying experience for fans of supernatural fantasy who don't mind a few clichés.

I recommend it to anyone looking for a fun anime featuring great character interactions, magical battles, and a story that is relatively easy to follow. Tokyo Ravens is nothing extraordinary, but it makes good use of its strengths to provide an enjoyable experience.

I also really liked the music. Both the opening and ending themes were enjoyable, and the soundtrack contributed to the atmosphere of the journey. Some scenes were especially effective because of the music accompanying them, which could make an already mysterious or melancholic moment even more striking.

Unfortunately, my viewing experience wasn't entirely straightforward. After watching the first six episodes, I had to take a break of almost two days because I wasn't feeling well. When I returned to the anime, I was worried that I wouldn't be able to get back into the same mood as before. However, it didn't take me long to regain my previous level of enjoyment and curiosity, and I was soon back to watching the episodes, writing down my thoughts and questions, and enjoying the series as I had before the break.

The final episodes gave me more information about some of the mysteries I had been wondering about, but they also left me with plenty of questions. I was especially interested in how the different pieces of information related to one another and what they might mean for the story as a whole. By the time I finished the twelfth episode, I still wanted to know much more. The ending left me wanting to continue the journey, and I was very aware that there was more to the story than the anime had been able to cover. Knowing that the manga is still ongoing made the prospect of finding all the answers even more uncertain, but it also left me curious about what might come next.

Overall, Touring After the Apocalypse was an incredible experience. I loved its intriguing story, the mysteries surrounding its world, the journey itself, the characters and their interactions, the artwork, and the music. It constantly gave me things to wonder about, and I found myself writing far more notes than I had ever expected to write for an anime outside of a rewatch. I don't think I have often been this engaged in recording my questions, observations, and theories while watching a series.

Despite the difficulties that affected my viewing experience, I'm extremely satisfied that I chose this anime. It was a beautiful, fascinating, and thoroughly enjoyable experience, and I'm very glad I watched it. I would also like to read the manga someday, especially because I want to learn more about the world and the many questions that remain unanswered.

Dirty Pair Flash is an incredibly entertaining sci-fi anime that excels in style, action, and character charisma. Its futuristic setting, gorgeous visuals, and fantastic soundtrack create an experience that captures everything great about '90s cyberpunk anime. Kei and Yuri are easily the biggest highlights. Both girls are hot, badass, confident, and take absolutely no nonsense from anyone. Their personalities and chemistry make them a joy to watch, while their excellent voice acting brings their characters to life, also they are both exceptionally funny! The futuristic worldbuilding is another major strength, with fascinating technology and sci-fi concepts that give the setting plenty of appeal. The visuals are outstanding,featuring vibrant colours, stylish character designs, and fantastic action sequences as you would expect from the golden age of Sunrise. Combined with an amazing soundtrack, the audiovisual presentation is an absolute treat.

Dirty Pair Flash delivers charismatic heroines, exciting action, cool futuristic lore, and an unmistakable '90s anime aesthetic.

Verdict: A stylish, action-packed sci-fi adventure carried by two fantastic leading ladies. An absolute blast from start to finish!

The first thing i will say about this anime is that it is most definitely a product of it's time. It is OVERWHELMINGLY 2006 to a decent degree, but I do feel that is does set the stage for what it meant to be a hikikomori at that time... especially compared to what that might look like nowadays. It's almost the perfect time setting for it though, funnily enough. Almost every aspect of this show is touched on fully: why the characters do the things they do, why they are the way they are, and most of all, their progressions. Sato, the MC, is not agreat person. I would even go as far as to say he is quite a pathetic individual at the start of the show - that may be harsh, but I do not think there's any kinder word to describe him after the first ~4 episodes. His character development though, is refreshingly realistic and doesn't fall into the trope of him suddenly improving because he has been struck by some silver bullet. He takes one step forward, two steps back constantly but you root for him because you know that he's not bullshitting about his mental state.

Misaki is a very odd character that fits seamlessly in the context of this show. Shrouded in mystery, it feels like at many times there is no rhyme or reason for why she does the things she does, but nonetheless she is still captivating in that she takes an interest in the MC that is not properly explained by a romantic attraction. To avoid spoilers, I won't dwell on that relationship further. She is somewhat enigmatic, predictable in her actions but impulsive in her reactions. And, the show does remind you at several points that she is just a young girl who is not as self-assured or even happy as she portrays herself to be. Her character really works here.

Yamazaki is almost like a Sato-lite, except that he does not share the same delusions as Sato about his current state of life and what will improve his quality of life. Otakumaxxing, sure, but he is relatable in the sense that he is held a victim to things outside of his control while he does make some missteps of his own making too. Cynical and irritable, Yamazaki is a perfect foil to Sato's character as while they do share a decent amount of similarities, he does not enable his hikikomori behaviour and outright makes actions to curb that trait in Sato, although not in an overtly altruistic way. His own misadventures in his personal life with that girl, and his school overall, is also engaging.

Hitomi is an interesting character. If you hear that this show is about conspiracy theories and cults, it would be because of this her role in the story. She is a senpai to Sato and thus is immediately held to some sort of elevated "status" above him in the beginning of the story, especially when you consider her life in the present. But of course, things are not as they seem and this is alluded to in the flashbacks.

A quick aside here to say that I adore the OST for this series. The intro is almost unskippable for me and the soundtrack throughout the series does speak to the experiences you are seeing on the screen rather than something that totally does not reflect the mood.

Critique? For one character's progression they take a bit long to get to the "why they do the things they do" part, and at times you watch what Sato is doing and say "come on bro". I guess the latter is to be expected though. Outside of those four characters, there is not much to speak of when considering the wider supporting cast. For the "third girl", I understood the situation but I did not really find myself as invested in her story as I did the other four characters. 

Should you watch this show? Yes.

The Twelve Kingdoms was an anime I was interested in watching, based on its trailer, as I usually do when choosing an anime to watch. I went into it with genuine curiosity, few expectations, and knowing very little about it beforehand, without any hype or external influence. I only assigned a score because it was required to publish this review. From the first episode, I found it interesting. The story managed to engage me even when I took long breaks between episodes, sometimes because I was tired or doing something else. I didn't necessarily feel an overwhelming urge to watch the next episode immediately, but whenever Ireturned to the anime, I found myself interested in what was happening and concerned about Youko and the other characters. Even the early episodes offered plenty of interesting moments, and the story kept me engaged throughout much of its first half.

One of the aspects I appreciated most was the worldbuilding. I was particularly interested in learning how this world worked, its history, its inhabitants, and the various concepts and mysteries surrounding it. There were many things I wanted to understand better, including aspects of the world's origins and how certain things came to exist. I also liked that the connection between the two worlds wasn't limited to the main characters travelling between them. The possibility of other people crossing between worlds, as well as the concern surrounding those who disappeared, made this aspect of the story more interesting to me.

I also enjoyed seeing the characters develop and change throughout the series. Youko, Suzu, Shoukei, Sugimoto, and others all had their own experiences and development, and I appreciated being able to follow their journeys. The characters were one of the anime's strengths, alongside its setting and the story it initially seemed to be building towards.

The series also had several emotional moments, alongside countless sad, dramatic, and heavy ones. There was at least one moment of this kind in every episode, and some episodes affected me more than others. Despite the difficult situations the characters faced, I generally found the story compelling, particularly during its first thirteen episodes, which were the most interesting and engaging part of the anime for me.

Unfortunately, my interest gradually diminished as the series progressed. Although the episodes following the recap around the middle of the series still had interesting moments, I didn't find them as engaging as the earlier ones. Some parts felt less interesting than they could have been, and I was increasingly disappointed by how certain storylines were handled.

One of my biggest disappointments was Asano. I felt that the character was largely wasted, especially considering how little he appeared throughout the series and how little we learned about what happened to him during his long absence. His eventual fate made this even more disappointing to me. I think the character could have been handled much better, and I was left feeling that a lot of potential had been wasted.

I was also disappointed by the way the anime handled its worldbuilding in the long run. Although the existence of twelve kingdoms initially made the world feel vast and full of possibilities, several of them received very little attention, while others were explored only briefly. I would have liked to learn much more about these kingdoms and the people who ruled them. Given how much potential the setting had, it was a shame that the series didn't make better use of it.

The later episodes were another major source of disappointment. I found the additional focus on En unnecessary, especially when there were other kingdoms and storylines that could have benefited from more attention. I understand that these episodes provide further background information, but I would have preferred to see the series use that time to explore other parts of its world. The final episode was particularly disappointing, as most of it recapped the preceding four episodes, leaving only the last few minutes for new material. This was an especially frustrating way to end the series after everything that had come before.

I also felt that the anime's visual presentation became less consistent as it progressed. The art direction in the later episodes often seemed noticeably weaker than in the earlier part of the series, although there were still moments when it looked good. There were also some instances of CGI that I found particularly poor. These issues further contributed to my disappointment with the later episodes.

As for the music, I gradually grew more accustomed to the opening theme, although it never really won me over apart from certain parts. The ending theme, on the other hand, grew on me as I continued watching, and I eventually came to like it.

Overall, The Twelve Kingdoms was an anime I liked, particularly for its characters, its worldbuilding, and the story presented in its earlier episodes. It had a setting that made me curious and a cast of characters whose development I enjoyed following. However, the unevenness of the later parts, the wasted potential of certain characters and storylines, and especially the final episode left me disappointed. I think the series could have made much better use of its world and the time available to it.

Prism Rondo is a beautiful anime, but I have mixed feelings about its romantic writing. What I loved most was how it used art to express emotions. Lili's development as an artist, the visual symbolism, and the friendships were genuinely wonderful. Watching her discover her own artistic identity was especially rewarding. However, my biggest issue was the unnecessary melodrama in Lili and Kit's relationship. The story already had meaningful conflicts involving family expectations, social class, war, and separation. It didn't need so many repeated misunderstandings and unspoken feelings. I was also deeply uncomfortable with the slapping scenes. Physical violence shouldn't be romanticized or turned into a recurring joke.The fact that the first incident was never properly addressed made its repetition even more frustrating.

Another major issue was how Kit was written. Despite being one of the main characters, he often felt more like a supporting character in Lili's story. His father's death, his experiences during the war, and his emotional struggles deserved much more attention. We spent so much time understanding Lili's feelings, yet Kit's perspective was frequently overlooked.

I loved the artistic symbolism and found the ending touching, but a beautiful conclusion doesn't erase the writing problems along the way.

Overall, Prism Rondo is a visually stunning and emotionally engaging anime with wonderful friendships and character development. I just wish its romance and Kit's character had been written with the same care.

Yet another set of extra episodes for Kuroko no Basket! Kuroko no Basket NG-shuu is a collection of short special episodes that serve as supplementary content to the main series, without significantly impacting the plot. Released alongside the Blu-ray and DVD versions, these episodes act essentially as a bonus for fans, offering comedic situations and lighthearted moments featuring the characters we’ve followed throughout the show. The concept here is simple: set aside the competition, intense matches, and player rivalries to focus on absurd scenarios, playful antics, and interactions that likely wouldn't fit into the main storyline. It’s interesting to see this more relaxed side of the cast,especially given their distinct personalities and dynamic, which can yield entertaining moments when they are placed in situations outside the norm.

However, while I understand the intent behind these specials, I have to admit the humor didn't quite work for me. Although there are some interesting scenarios and it’s pleasant to see the characters in a lighter context, many of the jokes failed to elicit as much laughter as I’d hoped. At times, I felt the characters' comedic potential could have been better utilized, making some segments feel more forgettable than truly entertaining.

I believe part of this feeling stems from the very identity of Kuroko no Basket. While the series does feature comedic moments, it stands out primarily for the intensity of its matches, the rivalries between players, and the way it builds conflict. Even its visual presentation, with its striking use of shadows and dramatic expressions, helps convey an atmosphere of seriousness and tension. Consequently, when these specials abandon much of that identity to focus almost exclusively on humor, I feel something gets lost in the process. That doesn't mean the episodes are bad or lack value. On the contrary, they offer a chance to spend more time with charismatic characters and explore interactions that make the cast feel even more familiar to long-time viewers. It is bonus content that will likely appeal to fans who enjoy seeing their favorite characters in everyday situations, free from the constant pressure of basketball matches.

The problem, for me, is that this format struggles to sustain interest on its own. The comedy isn't consistent enough to make every episode memorable, and the absence of what I consider the series' main draw results in a merely average experience. Ultimately, while it’s nice to watch these little extras, they don't add much to the overall Kuroko no Basket experience.

Overall, Kuroko no Basket NG-shuu is a pleasant supplement, created specifically for those who want to see the cast in more laid-back settings. I wouldn't call it a bad experience, but I can't recommend it with much enthusiasm either, especially to anyone looking for something that maintains the intensity and atmosphere of the main series. If you’re a Kuroko no Basket fan and are curious, it’s worth a look; otherwise, I don't consider it essential viewing.

Raiting: 5/10.

Premise: I chose Hanayamata based on its trailer, as I usually do when choosing an anime to watch. I went into it with genuine curiosity and few or no expectations, without any hype or external influence. I only assigned a score because it was required to publish this review. Hanayamata turned out to be a truly special experience for me. I was happy with my choice from the very first episode, which was both beautiful and genuinely funny. As I continued watching, the anime kept making me laugh and moving me emotionally, throughout the series. One of the things I loved most about this anime was its humour.There were countless funny moments, and even the short interludes and previews could make me laugh. I often found myself laughing so much that I would say “enough” while still laughing, not because I wanted it to stop, but simply because I couldn't help reacting that way. It's difficult to explain, but it was part of what made watching this anime such a particular experience for me.

At the same time, Hanayamata wasn't just funny. It also managed to move me in every episode, sometimes more intensely than others. The eleventh episode was especially emotional: there were several moments when I came close to crying, and from a certain point onwards, I was left feeling sad rather than amused. I was still feeling that way when I started the final episode, which managed to make me emotional again shortly after it began. Even so, the anime continued to make me laugh as well. Being able to make me experience both emotions throughout its entire run was something I found truly special.

I also really liked the characters. They were well characterised and felt realistic, and I thought the people behind the anime had done an excellent job bringing them to life.

Naru's development was another aspect I appreciated. By the final episode, I couldn't help noticing how much she had changed since the beginning. Her development felt gradual, with changes that became apparent from one episode to the next, rather than something that happened all at once.

The opening and ending themes were also among my favourite aspects of the anime. I loved both the songs and their visuals.

The voice acting was excellent as well, and it contributed to how much I liked the characters. Overall, I felt that a great deal of care had gone into the anime, and I appreciated the work that had been done across these different aspects.

I was also disappointed at the thought of having to wait an unknown amount of time before being able to read the manga, as I would love to see more of these characters and find out what their future holds.

Hanayamata was a genuinely special experience for me. It made me laugh and feel emotional in every episode, and left me with an ending that made me want to applaud. I had no trouble deciding whether I liked it; the difficulty was finding a way to express just how much the experience meant to me.

Even though I knew how much I had enjoyed Hanayamata, I struggled to decide what score to give it. I ultimately decided not to assign one, as I didn't feel that a score would do justice to my overall experience. However, after watching the finale, I realised that I would have given it a 10/10. The ending was wonderful, and I was so happy with the experience that I applauded continuously throughout the entire ending theme, from beginning to end.

entry.title: Mushoku Tensei: Isekai Ittara Honki Dasu Part 2

results.review:
It was a hard watch, until I told myself to separate me from the media, “I am not the arts I am consuming, I shall not project, to only observe as a by-stander”. And it become easier to take it. This part 2 is definitely a step-up in term of story-telling, environment building, characters development. The world is much more vast, the stakes are higher, and you faced moral questions which it tried to make you join one side and flip it to the other perspective and pull you to the other. I love that it explored other races and their traits, alongside with their loreinto great details. I am now very interested in this magical world and how it will become. 

It’s hard to give you reasons why I like it without spoilers, but few key moments I like is:
1. There were this “gambler” that was conveniently placed with Rudeus while he was caught in the Animal-human village. I always thought that this guy was a random character and a device for the author to try tying loose ends, but hearing his cheekyness and the way this guy laugh, I can’t help but connecting him to a certain white figure. It never said or imply in the SS1, but after I made the connection that this guy is not a normal person, my interest spikes and my mind was more determined to figure this out. It might be deeper than I thought
2. Roxy got back to her home and we found out why she was avoiding everyone. At first I thought: this isn’t that big of a problem, just talk to everyone! Then I realized how she couldn’t do that, and I realized what I did when I was 16 years old, and then when she wanting to leave right after she saw her parents speaking after just reunion with them, it clicks with me: It is that hard to bring yourself forward in a world of people not understanding you.
3. Rudeus and his father gathering was truly a surprise serious moment and I enjoyed it very much. No one was wrong at all.

And even more moments than this. Overall, I think it’s a very strong world-building and writing, that beside great fantasy elements, exploring human nature while tossing in jokes here and there make this show enjoyable. (Though I do wish Rudeus can tone down his lecherousness.)

Wasted opportunity. The idea of the show seems very cool, an elite human team that fights Mononoke, humans with special abilities and mononoke displaying all kinds of crazy magic, but is hugely underdeveloped. The humans don't really show of many abilities, they are basically strong and fast, with some high tech, they should have some cool powers. The plot is rushed, they basically go against the big evil in 12 episodes, this is maybe due to the new format in anime nowadays, that left so little room for developing stories well. The drawing looks pretty nice, but there's barely any animation, in fights don't expectto see connecting moves or anything amazing.

I don't know why they picked this one up to do a series, the manga is cancelled and I do not see any room to create a more interesting story here, they would have to remade a lot.

Premise: I chose Mob Psycho 100 based on its trailer, as I usually do when choosing an anime to watch. Although the trailer itself didn't particularly interest me, I was curious about the art direction, which ultimately became the aspect I appreciated most. The art direction was quite beautiful in some places, especially at the beginning, but in other parts it looked much more ordinary. This difference was already noticeable in the trailer, and I found it particularly striking when comparing the backgrounds and scenery. I also didn't care for the art direction during the comedic moments or for some of the characters' facial expressions. Evenso, it was the strongest aspect of the anime for me.

The story didn't interest me from the very first episode, and the characters didn't do much for me either. There were some things that reminded me of other works, but nothing that made me particularly interested in seeing more. As the episodes went by, I kept wondering whether the anime would eventually become more interesting or whether it would continue in much the same way. Unfortunately, my experience remained largely unchanged.

I found many of the ideas and messages presented throughout the series rather obvious. Some of the things said about everyday life and human behaviour were things I already knew, so they didn't give me much to think about. There were moments when I wondered whether these lessons would ever stop. I can understand why these aspects might appeal to other viewers, but they didn't do much for me.

As I continued watching, indifference became the word that best described my experience. Although there were moments when I felt differently, I was indifferent for most of the series. There were occasional moments that made me smile or laugh, but they weren't enough to change my overall impression. I often found myself with little to say about an episode beyond the fact that it hadn't particularly interested me.

The action sequences didn't change that impression either. I never came across a fight that impressed or surprised me, and I kept wondering whether there would eventually be one that stood out. By the end of the season, I still hadn't found one. I had seen people praise the action in Mob Psycho 100, so I wondered whether I was missing something, but the fights in this season simply didn't appeal to me in that way.

I didn't particularly like the opening song, although some of its visuals were nice. The ending theme, on the other hand, was visually beautiful, even though the song itself didn't do much for me. Overall, the music and sound were okay, but nothing more than that.

By the end of the season, my overall impression hadn't changed much from the beginning. The story hadn't become more interesting to me, the characters hadn't managed to capture my interest, and I didn't enjoy the fights. The art direction remained the strongest aspect, but it wasn't enough to make the anime an enjoyable experience for me.

I can understand why Mob Psycho 100 appeals to so many people, but I didn't find much in it that interested or engaged me personally. Still, I wouldn't describe it as one of the worst anime experiences I've had.

As an overall score based on my experience, I gave it a 3.4/10.

This anime is a simple romance with great execution, the anime's starring point is its absurd humor, specifically highlighted by the exaggerated overthinking of the main character Raidou, weird quirkiness across characters that makes each of them unique, and overall a cute romance. This season in specific highlights more of a slice of life feel in comparison to the first, which makes for solid entertainment but overall story becoming more bland. So this season in particular highlights wholesome moments and pushes more of the side characters involvement throughout the series, which can be great and unfortunate at the same time, some jokes are funny, cheesy,and kinda just suck, and the anime often rides the joke for a good portion of an episode which can make it very hit or miss.

Premise: I chose Akebi's Sailor Uniform based on its trailer, as I usually do when deciding which anime to watch. I went into it with genuine curiosity and few or no expectations, without any hype. From the very beginning, I found this anime beautiful. Its art direction is outstanding, although the CGI was a significant drawback for me, as it often is with anime. Some shots and artistic choices also worked better than others, but these issues never stopped me from appreciating the series as a whole. There were already plenty of funny moments in the first episode, and I quickly grew fond of the characters. Kaowas particularly surprising to me. I can't remember seeing a younger sister quite like her before, and I found her behaviour both amusing and endearing. Komichi, Kao, and their mother also struck me as a wonderful family. Their interactions felt genuine and natural, and I was delighted to see a family portrayed in this way.

However, what impressed me most was how real the characters felt. Each girl has her own personality, interests, and peculiarities, and the way they interact with one another feels so natural and believable that, at times, it seems as though I'm watching real people rather than fictional characters. Even the less conventional aspects of their personalities contribute to this impression. I never expected the series to achieve this level of realism, and it made me appreciate the author's work even more.

The sixth episode, in particular, left me speechless. Everything that happened at Komichi's home felt so natural, genuine, and realistic that it was almost as though reality itself had been turned into an anime. I found myself completely absorbed in what I was watching, and I couldn't stop thinking about how incredible the whole experience was.

My appreciation for the series only grew as I continued watching. Even when I was tired, distracted, or struggling to concentrate, it managed to draw me in and make me laugh, feel emotional, and become interested in what was happening. For personal reasons, I found it difficult to watch the ninth episode and had to take several breaks, some of them quite long. Despite this, I still found the episode beautiful and hilarious. I couldn't believe how consistently wonderful this anime remained, even when I was struggling to concentrate on it.

The final episode was nothing short of astonishing. I was left speechless for almost the entire episode, and I could feel my heart pounding throughout most of it. I was completely absorbed in what I was watching.
